I've long been fascinated with restaurant/retail automation and the design of vending machines. They seem to me a kind of performance art. One of the interesting things about the history of automation in fast food is how we actually went backwards in this because of the evolution in money rather than technology. Fast food as an industry really got its start in the US with diners and Automats which employed a very simple approach to automating the front-end of the restaurant operation that was, for a long time, very successful. Food was prepared and stored in little coin-operated cabinets the customer could access as they pleased. But after WWII they ran into a problem. Rising costs of food made paying for it with coins increasingly cumbersome while the government dragged its feet on implementing higher value coins. It would be some time before reliable paper bill scanner technology would develop, so humans were put back into the front-end largely to handle paper money, while also facilitating the use of drive-through and drive-in access.

Today we see a lot of talk about the automation of fast food restaurants through touch-screen ordering, but this is by no means new. The technology for this existed and was experimented with as much as 40 years ago and its cost was not much greater than it is today. Why has it taken until now to become attractive to fast food chains? Paper bill scanning is relatively reliable today, but still pretty cumbersome, frequently confounded by old bills, and often slower than human cashiers. And the elderly still have a hard time with computer interfaces that are overly 'modal', even on touch-screens. But one critical thing that has changed recently is the ubiquity of debit card use, particularly within the demographic for fast food customers. So now this automated front end is really practical since there's no currency to handle at all.

Recently a restaurant in San Francisco specializing in bowl meals called Eatsa has reintroduced a kind of Automat model with a touch-screen front end. People order by touch screen and food is put in digitally locked cabinets for customer access when the food is prepared. With this sort of model the touch screen, the debit card, and any on-site ordering almost become redundant in our age of smart phones and tablets as any ordering interface can be replicated as an app or web page. Of course, we already have on-line ordering for delivery foods and recently some places, like Subway, have introduced apps for pre-ordering. But one could easily go farther combining this with the Automat-like digital key cabinet. And so the front-end of some fast food restaurants could be nothing but an app and a walk-up wall of digital lockers which could be managed by fairly conventional automated materials handling systems. And all this is really not about the evolution of robotics but the evolution of money.
